section.title: The Two Ways
section.sectionRationale: An untitled wisdom psalm placed as the gateway to the whole Psalter. It teaches by contrast rather than narrative: the blessed man rooted in God's law against the wicked who are rootless chaff, a frame for reading every psalm that follows.
section.thesis: The blessed life is rooted delight in the LORD's law, fruitful and enduring like a tree by water, while the wicked life has no root and cannot stand in the judgment.
section.frameNote: Two portraits: the blessed man who delights in the law, pictured as a fruitful tree (vv1-3), and the wicked, pictured as chaff, with the LORD's verdict on both ways (vv4-6).

units.label: The blessed man
units.note: delight in the Law of the LORD

verses.text: {{ashre|Blessed}} is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, or set foot on the path of sinners, or sit in the seat of mockers.
But his delight is in the {{torah|Law}} of the LORD, and on His law he meditates day and night.
He is like a tree planted by streams of water, yielding its fruit in season, whose leaf does not wither, and who prospers in all he does.

units.label: The wicked and the verdict
units.note: chaff driven off by the wind

verses.text: Not so the wicked! For they are like chaff driven off by the wind.
Therefore the wicked will not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous.
For the LORD guards the path of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish.

ashre.gloss: Blessed, happy, the fortunate condition of one who lives rightly before God. It is a pronouncement rather than a wish: this is the person to be envied. It opens both the Psalter, Psalm 1:1, and the Sermon on the Mount, Matthew 5:3-11, joining wisdom's blessedness to kingdom blessedness.

torah.gloss: Instruction, law, teaching, the LORD's whole revealed will for life, not merely a list of rules. The blessed man's delight and meditation rests here day and night, the mark of true wisdom, echoed at length in Psalm 119.

basic.context: Psalm 1 stands as the gateway to the whole Psalter. It is an untitled wisdom psalm, more a meditation than a prayer, that sets before the reader two ways: the blessed path of delight in God's law and the way of the wicked that ends in ruin. It teaches how to read everything that follows.
basic.hermeneutics: This is wisdom literature, not narrative or prophecy, so it teaches by contrast rather than by reporting an event: two paths, two destinies. People debate whether the righteous man pictured here is sinless; the psalm itself assumes ordinary believers who still delight in God's word rather than the perfectly flawless.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalm opens with ashrei, blessed, a pronouncement of true happiness, centered on torah, God's instruction, which the blessed one loves enough to meditate on day and night. The wicked, by contrast, are chaff, dry husks with no root and no weight, blown away at the first wind.
basic.typology: The tree planted by streams of water, always fruitful and never withering, points forward to Christ, the truly blessed man who perfectly delighted in His Father's law and was never uprooted, and by union with Him believers become fruitful trees themselves.
basic.christ: Jesus is the one man who never walked in the wicked's counsel, never stood in the way of sinners, never sat with mockers, whose whole life was delight in His Father's law. He is Psalm 1's blessed man in full, and all who are united to Him by faith share His fruitfulness and are spared the coming judgment.
basic.god: God is the quiet gardener behind this psalm: He guards the path of the righteous, and under His judgment the wicked cannot stand. He is named only once, but every verb of blessing and every verdict of the last day belongs to Him.
basic.crossReferences: Jeremiah 17:7-8 pictures the same tree planted by water. Matthew 7:24-27 echoes the two ways and two foundations. Galatians 5:22-23 describes the fruit that grows from a life rooted in the Spirit.
basic.oneStory: Psalm 1 opens the Psalter with the Bible's oldest choice: the way of life, rooted in God's word, or the way of death, rootless and blown away. Every psalm after this is sung by someone walking one of these two ways, and the whole Bible resolves the choice in Jesus, the truly blessed man who makes His people fruitful trees.

context.literary:
The psalm is built on a hinge. Verses 1 to 3 describe one person and verses 4 to 6 answer with a single sharp phrase, "Not so the wicked!" Everything before it is a portrait; everything after is a foil. The first verse is itself a small staircase. The blessed man does not walk with the wicked, stand in the way of sinners, or sit among mockers, and the three verbs move from passing by, to lingering, to settling in. The company changes on the same downward step, from the wicked, to sinners, to mockers, people who have stopped merely doing wrong and now scorn the very idea of right.

The positive half turns on the small word "but" in verse 2. The man is defined less by what he refuses than by what he wants: his delight is in the Law of the LORD. Verse 3 then gives the payoff in one long picture, a planted tree, and verses 4 to 6 set against it the picture of chaff. Tree and chaff are the same kind of thing, a plant, and one has a source of water while the other has been cut from its stalk and stripped of every root. The psalm ends where it began, with the word "way," and the last line is a verb of ruin: the way of the wicked will perish.

The psalm has no title and no author's name. It sits first because it tells the reader what kind of book this is. The Psalms are a book of songs, but Psalm 1 asks that they be read as Torah, something to be taken in and turned over day and night. It is also paired with Psalm 2. Psalm 1 opens with "blessed" and Psalm 2 closes with "blessed," so the two together enclose a single frame, first the individual and then the nations, first the law and then the king.
context.historical:
Nothing in the psalm fixes a date or a speaker, and that silence is deliberate. A song that names no crisis can be prayed in any generation. The likely setting is the life of the covenant community after the Law of Moses had been given and was being read and taught, which is why the psalm assumes the Torah as a settled treasure the reader can meditate on.

The picture of a tree by water would have struck its first hearers with special force. Most of the land of Israel depends on seasonal rain, and in the dry months many streams run out. A tree beside a channel of water that never fails is the opposite of a farmer's anxious year. Chaff, the papery husk of the grain, is what the winnowers threw up into the evening breeze on the threshing floor, so that the heavy grain fell and the husk blew off. Anyone who had watched a harvest knew the fate of chaff.

The vocabulary of the wise also belongs to this world. The counsel of the wicked, the way of sinners and the seat of mockers are the advice, the habits and the company of a people who could choose their teachers. Israel's own kings were commanded to keep a copy of the law by them and to read it all the days of their lives, Deuteronomy 17:18-19, and Joshua was told to keep the Book of the Law from leaving his mouth and to meditate on it day and night, Joshua 1:8. Psalm 1 takes that charge given to a king and a general and offers it to every believer.
context.canonical:
Psalm 1 is the front door of a book that the Jews eventually arranged in five parts, and it works as a doorframe for the whole. Its two words, "blessed" and "way," return across the Psalter. The book of the first collection closes with another blessing, Psalm 41:1, and Psalm 119 begins by praising those who walk in the Law of the LORD, Psalm 119:1-2, as though the whole longest psalm were an unfolding of the delight sung here.

Other prophets and wise men took up its images. Jeremiah uses the tree planted by water for the man who trusts the LORD, Jeremiah 17:7-8, and Psalm 92:12-14 places the flourishing righteous in the house of the LORD, still bearing fruit in old age. Proverbs presents the same two ways, the path of the righteous like the first gleam of dawn and the way of the wicked like the darkest gloom, Proverbs 4:18-19. Ezekiel sees trees whose leaves do not wither growing on both banks of a river that flows from the sanctuary, Ezekiel 47:12, and Revelation gives the finished form of that picture in a river of the water of life with the tree of life on either side, Revelation 22:1-2.

In the New Testament the Sermon on the Mount opens with the same word for blessing, Matthew 5:3-6, and closes with the two builders, the wise and the foolish, Matthew 7:24-27. John the Baptist speaks of the chaff burned up with unquenchable fire, Matthew 3:12, and Jesus takes the fruit-bearing tree into the picture of the vine and its branches, John 15:5-6. The psalm's two ways are the frame inside which the Bible's largest warnings and promises are set.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted his hearers to decide which sort of person they intended to become, and to see that the decision is made daily, in small choices about advice, company and appetite, long before it shows up in a public verdict. That is why the psalm begins with three prohibitions of the ordinary kind that a young person meets in any community: whose counsel to take, whose path to follow, whose seat to share.

He also wanted them to understand delight. The verb of verse 2 is not a duty but a desire. The blessed man does not put up with the Law of the LORD as a burden he must carry; he loves it. Meditation, in the Hebrew idiom, involved a low murmuring recital, so the picture is of a man who has the words so close to his mouth that they come out when he is alone. That is how the text becomes a source and not just a rule.

Finally the author meant to give a comfort that has an edge. To the tempted, the mocked and the poor who watch the wicked seem to prosper, the psalm says that the appearance is a matter of season. The tree bears fruit in its season, and the chaff has no season at all. The last verse gives the reason the two ways cannot be equal: the LORD knows one, and the other perishes.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes a kind of person and the outcome of his life; it does not itself issue commands. Nothing in it says "do not walk" or "do meditate." It invites the reader to see, and the invitation carries force because the picture is honest. That has to shape how the promise of verse 3 is heard. "Prospers in all he does" is a wisdom generalisation about the shape of a life rooted in God, in the way a proverb says how things tend to go, and not a guarantee that every blessed believer will find every project succeeding. Job, Jeremiah and the psalmist himself in other psalms are counter-examples in the same book. Read as a contract, the verse turns into a formula for wealth and produces bitterness; read as a description, it steadies a person who is being squeezed.

What carries forward as instruction is the direction of the desire. The believer is meant to arrange life so that the word of God is the thing he returns to, and to be careful about which voices set the agenda of his thinking. That is an application of the psalm, not a rule that it states.

debates.question: Is the blessed man every believer, or one perfect man?

views.label: Every believer who delights in God's law
views.case: The plain sense of the psalm is a type of person, not one individual. The verbs are the ordinary habits of an ordinary member of the covenant community, and the Psalter as a whole assumes sinners who are forgiven, Psalm 32:1. On this reading the psalm sets a pattern for the people of God.

views.label: Christ alone, in the first instance
views.case: Some Christian interpreters hear in the flawless portrait the one man who never strayed. The three prohibitions and the promise of unfailing fruit fit Jesus perfectly, and they argue that no other man has ever met them, so that the psalm points beyond any human singer.

views.label: Both, in order
views.case: The largest group holds that the psalm describes the ideal person of the covenant, that only Christ has ever lived it fully, and that believers share the blessing because they are joined to Him by faith, so the psalm works at two levels without contradiction.

debates.bearing: The psalm's own wording keeps it open to ordinary believers, and the New Testament unfolds it by bringing Christ into it, so the safest use is to hear it as a pattern for every believer whose fruitfulness rests on union with the one who lived it perfectly.

debates.question: Does the promise that he prospers in all he does mean worldly success?

views.label: Material prosperity is the promise
views.case: Some take verse 3 as a direct pledge that a person who is faithful in God's word will do well in business, health and family. They point to the language of harvest and to the covenant blessings of Deuteronomy.

views.label: A general pattern of wisdom
views.case: Others note that Israel's wise men state how life tends to go in a moral world without making every case a law. Job's suffering and the psalmist's own laments in the book that follows show that the just are often hard pressed.

views.label: Fruitfulness measured by God's purposes
views.case: A third reading takes prosperity to mean that a life rooted in God's word reaches the end for which it was made, bearing the fruit of character and good work, even where outward reward is delayed until the judgment of verse 5.

debates.bearing: The tree yields fruit in its season, and the psalm ends with the verdict of the LORD, so the promise is best held as confidence about how a life rooted in God ends, not as a ledger for this year.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with the verbs of verse 1. The Hebrew for "walk," "stand" and "sit" are the ordinary verbs of movement, and together they sketch a whole life: how a person goes about, what he stops for, and where he makes his home. The counsel of the wicked is etsah, the advice a person takes when deciding what to do. The "mockers" are letsim, and the word is a moral category in Proverbs, where the scoffer will not take correction, Proverbs 9:7-8.

The verb translated "meditate" in verse 2 is hagah. It has the sense of a low murmur, a sound made in the throat, and that is why it can describe a person reciting under his breath. The word turns up again in the very next psalm, in Psalm 2:1, where the peoples "plot in vain." The same verb is used of both the blessed man and the raging nations, and the contrast is in the object: one murmurs over the Law of the LORD, the other over rebellion. The difference between the two psalms is a difference of what the mind rehearses.

In verse 3 the tree is "planted," a participle that describes a tree that has been set in place, not one that grew by chance. The "streams" are channels of water, probably watercourses cut to bring the water where the tree stands. Nothing about the tree is accidental: someone chose where it stood. The picture is of a life placed beside a supply.

The chaff of verse 4, mots, is the light husk of the grain, and the psalm says the wind drives it away. It has no roots to hold it and no weight to keep it. Verse 5 says the wicked will not "stand" in the judgment, using the same verb as the "stand" of verse 1. The man who would not stand in the way of sinners finds the sinners unable to stand at all.

The last verse deserves a closer look. The word BSB renders "guards" is the ordinary Hebrew verb for "know," yada. Old Testament "knowing" is more than information; it is a relationship, as when God says of Israel that He knew them only of all the families of the earth. The LORD knows the way of the righteous, and the way of the wicked perishes, the same verb that describes what happens to the wicked in Psalm 2:12. The two psalms are stitched together by this verb: to perish in the way is the end of anyone who will not take refuge in Him.

typology.type: The tree planted by streams of water, Psalm 1:3
typology.fulfillment: The tree that never withers points to the one man whose life bore fruit in every season, Jesus, who called Himself the vine and His people the branches, John 15:5. A branch that stays joined to Him bears much fruit, and one that does not is thrown away and burned, John 15:6, which is the psalm's chaff. The type is fulfilled in Him as the source of the fruit, not merely the example. It falls short because a tree needs the streams to be fed, while Christ is Himself the water, the life that flows into those joined to Him.

The choice between the two ways is taken up by Jesus in the narrow gate and the wide, and in the wise and foolish builders, Matthew 7:24-27. The wise builder hears His words and acts on them; the foolish one hears and does not. The correspondence is direct: the man who delights in the Law of the LORD becomes the man who builds on the words of Christ. The escalation is that the Lawgiver Himself now stands at the fork, calling Himself the way, John 14:6. The type falls short in that the psalm can only point to a path; Christ walks it with His people.

John the Baptist promises that the coming one will clear His threshing floor, gather the wheat and burn the chaff with unquenchable fire, Matthew 3:12. The old winnowing scene becomes the picture of the final judgment. The psalm's line that the wicked will not stand in the assembly of the righteous is thus made concrete: the sifting is the work of Christ. The type falls short because the psalm gives only the verdict, while the gospel offers a way for the chaff to be made wheat, by repentance and by faith in Him before the day of sifting.

study.christ:
The New Testament lays the psalm alongside Jesus in three ways. The first is contrast: the blessed man is the one who does not walk, stand or sit with the wicked, and Jesus is that man without a single lapse. He was tempted in every way and did not sin, Hebrews 4:15. He took the counsel of His Father's word for every answer in the wilderness, Matthew 4:1-11, and He delighted to do His Father's will, an echo of the psalmist's delight in the Law.

The second is source. A tree planted by water lives because of where it stands, and Jesus says of Himself that He is the vine and that His people bear fruit only by remaining in Him, John 15:5. The psalm shows what a fruitful life looks like; Christ shows where the life comes from. The believer does not become the blessed man by a superior effort at meditation, but by being joined to the one who is.

The third is judgment. The psalm says the wicked will not stand in the judgment, verse 5, and the New Testament tells us who sits in it. The Father has entrusted judgment to the Son, and John the Baptist says His winnowing fork is in His hand, Matthew 3:12. The one who is the blessed man and the source of blessing is also the judge before whom the chaff cannot stand.

Care is needed not to force the whole psalm into a private prediction of Jesus. The psalm is addressed to every reader, and its first job is to draw the reader into delight in the LORD's Law. But the shape of the psalm, an ideal man, a source of life and a final sifting, is fulfilled in Jesus with a completeness that no other person can claim, and the reader who wants to be like the tree finds that the only way is to be found in Him.
study.god:
God is mostly offstage in this psalm, and that itself is a lesson. His name occurs only in verse 2, "the Law of the LORD," and in verse 6, where He is the subject of the closing verb. Between those two mentions everything is done by the man, the wind, the tree and the chaff. The psalm invites us to see that the God who is quiet in the picture is the one holding it together: He has given the Law that is the source of delight, and He is the one who knows the way of the righteous.

The psalm shows God as a revealer. He has spoken, and what He has spoken is something a person can love and turn over in the mind all day. He has not left the world to guess about righteousness. The Law is treated here as a gift and not as a trap, and that shapes worship: the right response to a God who has spoken is delight, not resentment.

The psalm shows God as knowing. The verb behind "guards" in verse 6 is the verb for knowing, and it tells us that God's care of the righteous is personal knowledge, not distant oversight. He is not a supervisor watching from far off; He knows the way of His people as a shepherd knows a flock.

It also shows God as judge. Verse 5 says the wicked will not stand in the judgment, and the psalm does not soften it. The same God who is intimately near His people is the one before whom mockers will not last. These are not two moods. The God who knows the way of the righteous is the God who stands against the way of the wicked, because His nearness and His justice come from the same holiness.

For worship this means the psalm is both an invitation and a sobering charge. We come to a God who loves to be known, whose word is sweet, and who keeps His own; and we come to a God who takes moral distinctions seriously, so that our delight in His word is never sentimental.

crossReferences.note: God tells Joshua to keep the Book of the Law in his mouth and meditate on it day and night, promising that he will prosper and succeed. Psalm 1:2-3 uses the same words for meditation and prosperity, so the psalm reads as the general offer of what was first said to a leader.

The king must copy the Law and read it all the days of his life so that he learns to fear the LORD. The psalm takes the discipline laid on a king and widens it to any person who wants to be like the tree.

Jeremiah speaks of the man who trusts in the LORD as a tree planted by waters that does not fear the heat and does not stop bearing fruit in drought. It sharpens the psalm's promise by naming the hard seasons the tree survives.

The righteous flourish like a palm and a cedar, planted in the house of the LORD, still bearing fruit in old age. It adds the setting of worship and the long haul: the blessed life is planted in God's presence and does not stop.

The path of the righteous is like the first gleam of dawn, growing brighter, while the way of the wicked is deep gloom in which they do not know what makes them stumble. The proverb takes the psalm's two ways and sets them in light and darkness.
John says the coming Christ will clear His threshing floor, gather the wheat and burn the chaff. The psalm's chaff driven by the wind becomes the final act of judgment in the hands of the Messiah.

Jesus ends the Sermon on the Mount with two builders. The wise one hears and acts, and the house stands; the foolish one hears and does not act, and it falls. It is Psalm 1's two ways told as a parable, with Christ's own words now the foundation.

Jesus is the vine and His people the branches. Those who remain in Him bear much fruit, and those who do not are thrown away like withered branches. It answers where the tree of the psalm gets its life.

The final line of the next psalm, 'Blessed are all who take refuge in Him,' answers the first word of Psalm 1. The two psalms make one frame around the entrance to the Psalter: blessed is the one who delights in the Law, and blessed is the one who takes refuge in the King.

The river of the water of life flows from the throne, with the tree of life on either bank, bearing fruit each month. The tree by streams in Psalm 1 finds its final form in the new creation, where the water never fails.

study.oneStory:
In the story of the Bible, Psalm 1 answers a question that begins in the garden. In Genesis 3 the man and woman chose to listen to another voice, and the counsel of the serpent became the first counsel of the wicked. Two ways opened from that moment, and Genesis 4 shows them already at work in Cain's line and in the line of Seth. Psalm 1 names those two ways and asks the reader to choose.

The rest of the Old Testament makes the choice concrete. Moses puts before Israel life and death, blessing and curse, Deuteronomy 30, and the prophets spend centuries describing a people who chose the wrong way and were driven, like chaff, into exile. Yet even in exile there is a remnant, and the psalm's tree survives in them, as in Jeremiah's man who trusts the LORD.

The psalm also sets up something it does not itself deliver. It describes a man who has never lived: one who never walks with the wicked, never wavers, whose delight in the Law is undivided. No child of Adam qualifies. The psalm therefore leaves the reader wanting a blessed man who has done it, and the next psalm supplies him, the Anointed King on Zion. In the gospel that man is Jesus, who meets every clause of Psalm 1 and then gives His life for those who did not.

The end of the story fulfils the picture literally. In Revelation 22 the river of the water of life runs from the throne of God and of the Lamb, with the tree of life on either bank, and its leaves heal the nations. The tree planted by the streams is no longer a single person's image; it is the shape of the whole restored creation. The chaff does not enter that city. The way of the wicked has perished, and the way of the righteous, which the LORD has known all along, ends at the tree of life.

sermon.title: Delighting in the Law of God
sermon.why: Piper preaches through Psalm 1's contrast between the blessed man who delights in God's law and the wicked who are like chaff, drawing out what it means to actually delight in Scripture rather than merely obey it.

quiz.q: What is the blessed man's defining mark in Psalm 1:1-2?

options.text: He does not walk with the wicked, and his delight is in the LORD's law, which he meditates on day and night.
options.note: Both the negative avoidance and the positive delight define the blessed life.

options.text: He avoids sinners and mockers entirely.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but it omits the positive heart of the psalm, delight in God's law.

options.text: He works hard and prospers financially.
options.note: The psalm's prosperity is about fruitfulness under God, not a formula for wealth.

options.text: He never sins.
options.note: The psalm does not claim sinlessness; it describes a life oriented toward delight in God's word.

quiz.q: What image describes the wicked in verse 4?

options.text: Chaff that the wind drives away, with no root and no weight.
options.note: This is the psalm's sharp contrast to the deeply rooted, fruitful tree.

options.text: A tree that has stopped bearing fruit.
options.note: Close in spirit, but the actual image given is chaff, not a fruitless tree.

options.text: A stone that cannot be moved.
options.note: This misreads the image; chaff is light and blown away, the opposite of an immovable stone.

options.text: A shepherd who has lost his flock.
options.note: This image is not in the psalm at all.

quiz.q: What happens to the wicked in the judgment, according to verse 5?

options.text: They will not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous.
options.note: The psalm states this plainly as the outcome of the wicked's rootless life.

options.text: They will eventually repent and be welcomed in.
options.note: A hopeful thought, but not what this verse states; the psalm's verdict here is exclusion.

options.text: They will be judged more leniently than the righteous.
options.note: The text says the opposite: they will not stand at all.

options.text: Nothing; the psalm has no final judgment.
options.note: Verse 5 explicitly describes a judgment and an assembly the wicked cannot enter.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament fulfill the picture of the blessed man?

options.text: Jesus Christ perfectly delighted in His Father's law and lived the blessed life in full, making His people fruitful trees by union with Him.
options.note: Christ fulfills the blessed man's pattern, and believers share His fruitfulness by faith.

options.text: Every believer automatically becomes sinless like the blessed man.
options.note: Union with Christ brings fruitfulness and standing, but not present sinlessness.

options.text: The blessed man is only a moral example with no connection to Christ.
options.note: This misses the deeper typological connection Scripture draws to Christ's own perfect obedience.

options.text: The New Testament never refers back to this psalm's imagery.
options.note: Jesus' own teaching on the two ways and Jeremiah's tree image both echo Psalm 1 directly.

quiz.q: What is the meaning of 'meditates' in verse 2?

options.text: A low, repeated murmuring or reciting of God's word, showing sustained, loving attention rather than a single reading.
options.note: The Hebrew hagah pictures ongoing, murmured reflection, not a single glance at Scripture.

options.text: Silent, purely mental reflection with no repetition.
options.note: Reflection is part of it, but the word specifically carries a sense of murmured repetition.

options.text: Memorizing the text once and moving on.
options.note: The picture is ongoing, day and night, not a single act of memorization.

options.text: A formal liturgical ceremony performed once a year.
options.note: This is not what the word or the verse describes.

questions: Psalm 1 begins with what the blessed man does not do before it describes what he delights in. Where do you need to step back from the counsel, path, or seat of those who scorn God, before you can delight in His word?

The blessed man meditates on God's law day and night, a picture of sustained attention, not a single reading. What would it look like for you to return to Scripture again and again this week rather than treating it as a box to check?

The tree is fruitful because it is planted by streams of water, not because it works harder than the chaff. How does this shape the way you think about spiritual fruit, as something that flows from being rooted, not from sheer effort?
Chaff has no weight and no root; it looks like part of the harvest until the wind comes. Where might you be relying on appearances of faith rather than genuine roots in God's word?

Jesus lived the blessed life perfectly on your behalf. How does knowing that your standing before God rests on His fruitfulness, not your own, change how you approach your own failures to delight in His law?

translationNotes.note: Ashrei, blessed, is grammatically plural in Hebrew, sometimes rendered 'oh, the blessednesses of' the one who lives this way, an intensified pronouncement of happiness rather than a simple wish.
Meditates renders hagah, a word that can mean to murmur, mutter, or growl low in the throat, describing the quiet, repeated recitation of memorized Scripture rather than silent study alone.
Chaff describes the light husk separated from grain at threshing and blown away by wind, a common ancient Near Eastern image for what has no lasting substance or value.
